title: Information Commission to hear RTI appeals again after two years
excerpt: Hearings restart on 16 November with a backlog of more than 900 complaints. The new commission also plans to watch how foreign donations are used.
content:
The Information Commission will resume hearing right to information (RTI) complaints and appeals on Monday, 16 November, after being largely inactive for more than two years, Chief Information Commissioner Prof Nahreen Islam Khan said in Dhaka on Thursday, 12 November, The Daily Star reported.

The commission had no members for most of that time. Its commissioners resigned or were removed after the July 2024 uprising, and no new commission was formed until 17 October 2026, Prothom Alo reported. Prof Khan, a professor of geography and environment at Jahangirnagar University, is the first woman to hold the post. Journalists SAM Mahfuzur Rahman and Khan Mohammad Abul Hossain are the two information commissioners.

The backlog

  • Complaints waiting: 917 received while the commission was inactive, according to The Daily Star; Prothom Alo put the figure at about 950.
  • Staff: 22 officers and employees against 76 sanctioned posts, The Daily Star reported. Prothom Alo gave 27 working against 68 approved posts.
  • Track record: 5,804 complaints were filed from 2009 to 2023, and 55.7% were accepted for hearing, according to Prothom Alo. Of 324 complaints accepted in 2023, 42 were against private organisations and the rest against government offices.
  • Requests answered: about 167,000 information requests were made up to December 2024, and applicants got the information in about 95% of cases, Prothom Alo reported.

The 100-day plan

Prof Khan presented a 100-day work plan. According to The Daily Star, it includes:

  • District-level offices from next year.
  • RTI fairs at universities and schools. Prothom Alo reported fairs at six universities in December.
  • Training for journalists and content creators.
  • Monitoring government spending and the use of foreign donations.
  • Asking institutions to publish detailed information on their websites.

Commissioner Mahfuzur Rahman urged journalists who face obstacles in investigative reporting to seek the commission's help, and called for the RTI Act to be extended to the private sector, The Daily Star reported. The commission did not explain how it would monitor foreign donations.

Why it matters

The Right to Information Act 2009 covers NGOs that receive government or foreign funds, as well as public offices. A working commission means NGOs and citizens can again appeal when officials refuse information, but NGOs should also expect more requests about their own projects and funding. The plan to monitor foreign donations adds a second body watching NGO money, alongside the NGO Affairs Bureau.

What to watch

How quickly the backlog is cleared after hearings restart on 16 November, how the commission defines its role on foreign donations, and whether the government fills the vacant posts.
